The Young-Burgess system is useful for predicting transfusion requirements in pelvic ring fractures. For this system to predict mortality or non-orthopaedic injuries, fractures must be divided into stable (APC1, LC1) and unstable (APC2, APC3, LC2, LC3, VS, combined mechanism of injury) types.

To summarize:

- Stable fractures are typically defined as those that do not significantly compromise the stability of the pelvic ring.
- Unstable fractures, on the other hand, may have compromised stability and can be at increased risk for complications such as mortality or non-orthopaedic injuries.

It is essential to note that LC1 injuries are often very common and not always benign, with an overall mortality rate of 8.2%. 

While the Young-Burgess system does predict transfusion requirements in some cases, it is crucial to consider other factors such as patient comorbidities, overall health status, and the mechanism of injury when making treatment decisions.

Early intervention and appropriate management can significantly impact outcomes for patients with pelvic ring fractures.
